speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Singapore Public Service is made up of Ministries and Statutory Boards, which work together to deliver services to the public.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, Ministries, which are led by Ministers, are responsible for setting policy directions, while Statutory Boards focus on implementation to achieve the policy outcomes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Each Statutory Board has a constituting Act which spells out its powers and functions and the key governance requirements.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These Acts provide for the Statutory Boards to be separate legal entities from Ministries, and to be governed by their own Board of Directors.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This allows them greater autonomy over day-to-day running of operations, and ensure greater responsiveness, efficiency and effectiveness.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: To illustrate, Statutory Boards have broad discretion over operational issues, can exercise some flexibility over terms and conditions to hire employees, can own land and raise capital by issuing bonds.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: At the same time, Statutory Boards are part of the Government and cannot be totally independent either, and Ministers are ultimately accountable for their performance in Parliament.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: How Statutory Boards operate must, therefore, be in line with the policy directions set by Ministers and their Ministries.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They must also abide by important tenets of governance, such as standards of conduct and discipline, principles of remuneration, such as the clean wage policy, that apply to the whole Public Service.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In short, Statutory Boards are part of the Government, to be governed centrally, but deliberately constituted as separate entities for operational flexibility.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They have been set up over the decades.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The oldest Statutory Board in existence today is the Central Provident Fund (CPF) Board which was established in 1955.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: A few were constituted only last year, namely, Workforce Singapore, SkillsFuture Singapore, Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) and Government Technology Agency of Singapore (GovTech).

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Because of the considerable timespan during which different Statutory Boards were established, the key governance requirements in the Acts of our Statutory Boards are not even.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, all Statutory Boards already follow the same practices for good governance.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For example, most Statutory Board Acts provide for the Minister charged with the responsibility of the Statutory Board to approve the appointment of its Chief Executive (CE).

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: However, for the five polytechnics, their Acts do not make this requirement, even though in practice, the Ministry of Education (MOE) and the Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) search, shortlist, interview and bring about the appointments.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There is no reason for the polytechnics to be different from the other Statutory Boards in terms of legislative provisions.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This Bill pulls together and standardises four main areas of governance that are already present in most Statutory Board Acts.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: One, the power for the responsible Minister to give directions to Statutory Boards on the performance of their functions, with which they must comply.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Divisions 1 and 3 in Part 2 reflect this.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These directions must be consistent with written laws and cannot influence any statutorily independent or quasi-judicial functions of the Statutory Boards.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: To ensure impartiality of the Public Service, the Bill specifies that directions must not be given to achieve specific outcomes or to make employment decisions regarding a particular person or persons.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Two, personnel matters regarding the role, appointment, removal, promotion and discipline of the CEs of Statutory Boards are reflected in Division 1 of Part 3.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This Division, first, clarifies that other than proper administration and management of the functions of the Statutory Boards in line with Ministerial directions, the CE also has to collaborate with the wider Public Service to deliver public value.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is important because, as our challenges become more complex, they cannot be solved by one agency alone.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This change clarifies that agencies can go beyond a narrow interpretation of the functions described in their Acts to also support and seek support from other agencies, which they are already encouraged to do to achieve whole-of-Government objectives today.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In cases where the President’s concurrence is also required, such as the Fifth-Schedule Statutory Boards, it is a four-key system.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Three, the requirement for Statutory Board Governing Board members to disclose conflicts of interest, as reflected in Division 1 of Part 4.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This Part defines the circumstances under which a member of the Governing Board is deemed to be interested in a matter, and also the standard of disclosure.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These provisions are consistent with corporate governance practices adopted by the private sector and are already in the recently-passed Statutory Board Acts, such as the SkillsFuture Singapore Agency Act, the Government Technology Agency Act, and the recently amended Town Councils Act.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Four, finance-related requirements relating to the preparation and adoption of budget estimates, the keeping of proper accounts, audit requirements and the presentation of the audited financial statements and annual reports to Parliament.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These Part 5 provisions are basic requirements to ensure proper internal controls and governance over finance administration.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Now, let me move on to the second area: formalising today's administrative requirements to comply with key central policies.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Our Statutory Boards currently comply with a range of policies set by central agencies, developed in consultation with key stakeholders, such as the Statutory Boards themselves and public-sector unions.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, PSD issues directives on HR matters, and MOF on finance matters.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is reflected in Division 1 of Part 2.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Such central policies need to strike a balance between effective governance across the Public Service, and the flexibility Statutory Boards need for operational success.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For example, Statutory Board salaries are benchmarked to the talent markets they compete in, and we do not expect every Statutory Board to pay exactly the same salary or to have the same salary scales.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But it would be imprudent to allow Statutory Boards to have an absolute free reign in setting salary packages.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Hence, we have a process where Statutory Boards must consult their Ministries and the PSD when reviewing their salaries and take their views into consideration.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: During this process, we will ensure that salary benchmarks are appropriately set, the Statutory Board abides by the clean wage policy and so on.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Central directions by the relevant Ministers must likewise be consistent with written laws.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Directions cannot affect the performance of any statutorily independent or quasi-judicial functions of any Singapore public sector agency, including the Judiciary.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This would mean, for instance, that the directions cannot undermine the independence of the Judiciary guaranteed by the Constitution.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Courts will continue to exercise their judicial function independently, unimpeded by any Ministerial directions, and Court orders will have to be obeyed notwithstanding any requirement contained in a direction.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Directions cannot be given to achieve specific outcomes or to make employment decisions regarding a particular person or persons.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The use of data has transformed the way services are conceived and delivered to bring greater convenience and faster, more seamless service to users.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For example, when we drive, our location data is aggregated with the other drivers, shared with an app company to generate real-time traffic condition maps and to guide our travels.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Public Service is also using data to better serve the public, in two ways.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The first, is to better provide frontline service.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: One good example is the Ministry of Social and Family Development's (MSF’s) Social Service Offices (SSOs).

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: When a resident applies for financial assistance at an SSO, he does not need to submit various documents before receiving assistance.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The frontline officers already have access to data from multiple agencies to swiftly evaluate his or her eligibility for financial assistance.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Another example is MyInfo, a "tell-us-once" platform for Government services that the Public Service is currently developing.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: When an individual wants to perform an online Government service transaction, such as applying for a Housing and Development Board (HDB) Build-to-Order (BTO) flat, enrolment into polytechnics or applying for baby bonus, he or she needs to log in via SingPass, and MyInfo will automatically prefill the application form with his or her information.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is achieved by pooling an individual’s personal data from multiple agencies securely through a central platform, and the outcome is a more hassle-free and seamless online transaction process for the applicant.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Another way to improve public service is to use data for analysis and to develop policies and programmes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For example, Government agencies are using the Enterprise Data Hub (EDH), a central repository of business entity data, to better understand industries and companies, bring about better analytical insights and improved support strategies for industries and businesses.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In the case of MOE, we can put together data on past education attainment, family background, jobs and careers to better understand the relationship between education and careers.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But in doing such analysis, we need to anonymise the data because it is the aggregated trend and the causal relationships that we are seeking to understand.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Hence, we will set up centralised data custodians, where raw data from different sources will be matched and anonymised, before being released to relevant agencies for analysis.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Such cross-agency data sharing initiatives are already happening today because technology has made it possible.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But we need to strengthen the rules which were written before we could envisage how we can leverage data to improve our work and deliver services better.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is backed up by amendments to the Civil Service’s internal guidelines to further elaborate the conditions for sharing.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In gist, identifiable personal data is shared when services need to be better delivered to the individual, while non-identifiable data is shared to improve policy analysis, planning and formulation.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Second, under today's rules, there is an asymmetrical distribution of responsibility between data owning and data requesting agencies.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, it will actually enhance data security and safeguards.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For avoidance of doubt, the Bill makes it clear that sensitive data protected by legislation would remain protected.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This includes data exchanged or received by Statutory Boards, which are subject to confidentiality obligations under international treaties or agreements that are provided for under any written law.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: All the changes proposed in this Bill will generally apply to all Statutory Boards, except where there are grounds for exemption.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Exemption is due to the function of the Statutory Board and the context in which they operate.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For example, the National Council of Social Services (NCSS) is unlike regular Statutory Boards in that its main functions focus on developing the capabilities and representing the interests of the voluntary welfare sector and serving as a bridge between the Government and the sector.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As such, NCSS functions more autonomously from Government than regular Statutory Boards and is exempt from the requirement to obtain PSC’s concurrence in the appointment, removal, promotion and discipline of its CE.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Another group of Statutory Boards, like the Singapore Medical Council and the Land Surveyors Board, serve mainly to self-regulate the professional standards, training and conduct of their respective professions.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Their core functions relate to the exercise of professional judgement on licensing particular persons to practise as a professional in a field.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Governing Boards, therefore, comprise registered practitioners of relevant professions with autonomy to exercise professional judgement.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Hence, the Minister has a smaller role to play in their work and PSC is not involved in the appointment or removal of their Registrars.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The text of the Bill currently exempts the PA from: one, the power of the responsible Minister to give directions to PA; two, the role of the Governing Board and responsible Minister in appointing the PA's CE; and three, the requirement for the Chairperson to sign the PA's audited financial statements.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We had originally given the exemptions due to the unique constitution of the PA where the Prime Minister is the Chairperson while the responsible Minister is the Deputy Chairperson.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But we have since relooked the exemptions and decided to have consistency in PA's governance with the other Statutory Boards.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The only remaining exception is that volunteers who serve on PA's committees will not be subject to the protection as well as the offences that relate to public servants under the Penal Code, for the simple reason that they are volunteers.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: One, an amendment to the Interpretation Act, to set out the longstanding practice where subsidiary legislation made by a Statutory Board is signed by the chairperson.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This clarifies that the chairperson's signature is sufficient to indicate that a Statutory Board has passed that legislation in resolution without further need for all members to sign the legislation.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The amendment also clarifies that where a Statutory Board is permitted by any written law to delegate the performance of its functions or the exercise of its powers, this does not apply to the power to make subsidiary legislation.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This reflects the policy since January 2017 to stop grouping officers by divisional status to better emphasise skills and performance in the management of officers.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is in line with the national SkillsFuture movement.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This will improve the efficiency of our work processes and fairer to the officer, too.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Four, amendments to the PSC and Legal Service Commission (LSC) Act.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This inconsistency exists because the PSC and LSC Act was enacted in 1956 before the Singapore Constitution was enacted in 1963.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This will not affect the President’s powers, and we have consulted the President’s office before proposing to streamline our statutes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This Bill will strengthen the governance of Statutory Boards to better deliver services for the benefit of all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Streamlining processes in the Public Service would have obvious benefits to the public and make governance more efficient and effective.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: From a public perspective, it can be frustrating, and I know many residents as well as businesses are often frustrated when Government agencies lob them from department to department and sometimes even Members of Parliament (MPs) are not immune to this.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To make an application or appeal, one has to go online to different websites or to different departments to get the relevant documentation because the information among the different agencies cannot be shared.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I see many possibilities that data sharing can make living better for the under-privileged and those in need.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Very often, I have had residents coming to our Meet-the-People Sessions (MPS) for help, especially for welfare appeals, home purchases and other declarations needed, such as immigration applications, where documents and statements are asked each time they make an appeal, whether it is CPF records, income statements, certified medical certificates and so forth.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Too often, many give up on these schemes or benefits because of the long process and when data and document sharing becomes onerous.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The family situation for those in need is not always so straightforward.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Family members may be difficult to locate and sometimes family members are also estranged.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, systems can work in the background without having to reveal exact numbers to officers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, in a sense, you go to the backend, get certain data, churn out a formula and, therefore, a score comes out to say whether a resident is eligible or not eligible.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, officers making the assessments will see some form of points scoring to make it easier and quicker to approve one’s eligibility for a scheme.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This will allow officers to make decisions without having to access actual data.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For example, an agency can evaluate if an applicant’s household income exceeds the specified criteria through comparing CPF and/or Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS) data, without having to be given actual details which will breach some of our laws.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If the system can compute such a formula, this will help reduce trauma and difficulties by the applicant and reduce the burden on the processing for help.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This way, more citizens will get help more expediently and with much lesser stress.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The second consideration is the possibility of achieving cost-effectiveness.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In the sharing of data and making Government processes more efficient, would such services not become cheaper for the relevant agencies and, consequently, the public?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am not just talking about direct cost savings but also indirect savings in terms of neater allocation of resources, achieving optimal outcomes and leading to effective policy outcomes.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, I understand MyInfo is a good platform and I hope that more can be done, but also not in terms of pre-filling forms, when we were to carry forward some of these application data that was previously submitted.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In recent years, we have heard of many businesses attributing the low take-up rate of Government schemes and grants to complicated and long-drawn processes of such applications and reporting.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hopefully, we will see businesses more encouraged to do so now in light of easier data sharing among agencies, so they do not have to keep repeating their applications across agencies.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Last, but not least, the importance of taking concrete steps towards being a truly Smart Nation.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Data and, more importantly, the insights that can be garnered from it, are proving to be critical and significant in this digital era.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Companies and governments around the world are increasingly leveraging data to serve their customers and citizens better, and Singapore should leverage such capabilities to improve and enhance policymaking.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: After all, if we are truly driving Singapore towards being a Smart Nation, then the Public Service should be incentivised to lead by example.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I support this initiative to further our use of digital technology under our Smart Nation initiative, in areas that can better our lives, such as making our public transport services more efficient and enhancing our access to healthcare, amongst others.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, acknowledging these benefits, I would like to share the concerns I have on this Bill based on feedback gathered on the ground.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The main concern some have on this move is the perception that "big brother" is watching.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: While governance and transparency are areas to keep in mind, we need to be clear on whether the Government will make public on what datasets that the "directing" Minister has asked for across agencies, and what they will be used for.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is especially for datasets that will be used for proactive enforcement of citizens, if any, such as tax compliance or declarations.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: My other concern is the erroneous or non-updated data on an individual or business which could work against them when used by the Government to approve applications for schemes and services.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Also, given that Government officers now have access to a full suite of data, which, put together with reasonable deduction, may lead to market or sensitive insights and the possibility of what some may call "insider trading" for use of information for personal gain.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: While the Bill covers penalties for data leaks, I do have concerns that, in recent years, we have seen Auditor-General’s Office (AGO) reports where data and systems controls remain a concern for some agencies.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, what additional measures will be put in place in terms of data security?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Once data is leaked, even if we can penalise the officer, there is no retrieving the data back.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, I would like to know how the Government plans to balance security, governance and accessibility of data.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If these concerns are addressed, Mr Deputy Speaker, I am confident that the Bill brings greater convenience and efficiency to Singaporeans and the Public Service.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To this end, the Bill has several aspects.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On the one hand, it aims to standardise certain policies and practices that cut across the different public sector agencies, such as personnel matters, governance and managing conflicts of interests and financial administration.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These are set out in Parts 3, 4 and 5 of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These accountability provisions set out how Ministers should interface with public sector agencies which wield significant state power over Singaporeans on a daily basis, how should Ministers behave and what are the boundaries that Ministers should not cross.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I shall focus my speech on this aspect of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Are Ministers or the agencies confused about their roles?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Why legislate rather than issuing guidelines on this?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Is there concern from the Public Service officials that they are being subject to political pressure from Ministers?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Part 2 of the Bill talks about Ministers issuing directions to agencies.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I note that under clause 9, it is provided that the directions may take the form of a circular, instruction or order.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But clause 9 says that the directions may take such a format, not that they must take such a format.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Is it safe to assume then that directions have to be in writing and signed or authenticated by the Minister?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Can the Permanent Secretary, for example, sign off?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Is there anything prohibiting directions in the form of emails or going further, can directions even be oral?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Part 2 envisages two types of directions from Ministers – directions for whole-of-Government approach and directions to certain Statutory Boards regarding functional responsibilities.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Under clause 4, directions for the whole-of-Government approach will relate only to a pertinent subject matter.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These pertinent subject matters are restricted to five areas as set out in sub-clause (3).

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, employment, management and discipline of employees; second, management of official documents; third, financial and resource management and accountability; fourth, use or development of IT; and fifth, data governance and sharing.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such whole-of-Government directions are to be issued by, I presume, the Prime Minister's Office (PMO) or the recommendation of the Minister-in-charge of the pertinent subject matter.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In addition, the directions can only be issued for the purposes set out in clause 4(2), such as securing economies of scale, efficiency of public programmes, ensuring business continuity and managing financial risks.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Overall, I welcome the thought process behind clause 4 and the implied reminder to Ministers that directions should not be issued for extraneous purposes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Next, I move to directions to Group 1 Statutory Boards.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The second type of directions are to be issued under clause 5 to specific Statutory Boards on the performance of their specific functions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I also understand from the Minister that he would be moving an amendment in Committee to include the Group 1C public body, namely, PA, under clause 5 as well.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Clause 5 states that such agencies' specific directions are to be issued by the Ministers responsible for those agencies.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Implied here is a drawing of a line that other Ministers have no authority to give instructions to agencies not under their charge concerning the agencies' functions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In this regard, it would be important to understand the spirit behind this provision.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: According to the Explanatory Note, there are currently inconsistencies and this clause will help to avoid duplication of laws.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Could the Minister give an illustration of this problem so that one can better understand how clause 5 will help?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Next, I move on to limits on Ministerial directions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is contained in clause 11, an all-important clause which seeks to limit the Minister's powers to issue directions to public sector agencies.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Clause 11 provides that the Minister's directions must not be contrary to written law.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To enable greater public understanding of this point, can the Minister give some examples of such functions?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Earlier, I believe he mentioned the Courts, which are an obvious example.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But it would be helpful if he could mention other examples.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Furthermore, should there be a doubt as to whether a direction from a Minister is contrary to law or tantamount to an undermining of that body's independence or quasi-judicial function, how will such an issue be resolved?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Who should the public sector agencies complain to?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Next, clause 11(3) goes further to say that Ministers are not authorised to direct any public sector agency or any public body or public officer to perform or not to perform a particular act with respect to a particular person or persons.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Read literally, does this mean, for example, that henceforth, a Minister cannot direct a Statutory Board to scrutinise the accounts of a particular company?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Does this mean that Ministers cannot instruct Ministries or Statutory Boards to issue specific media releases affecting particular persons?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Next, which agencies are protected under this clause from Ministerial abuse?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Public bodies are also mentioned in clause 11 which means it protects all Statutory Boards, even those not listed in the Schedule.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To be absolutely clear, does clause 11 apply to the Public Service?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We just defined to include the Singapore Armed Forces (SAF), the Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF) and the Police.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Are these considered departments of the Government and, therefore, public sector agencies for the purposes of this Bill?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is important because if clause 11 applies to the services, a Minister would not be able to direct them to take particular actions, for example, to direct the Police to arrest a particular person.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But with the public sector that has known only one ruling Party for nearly 60 years, how do we entrench a culture of political neutrality of the Civil Service in substance?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, buried in our Statute Books is a piece of legislation called "The People Association's conduct and discipline rules".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These rules expressly state that, I quote, "Every employee shall refrain from engaging in party political activity and shall maintain complete reserve in all matters of party political controversy." Besides this, I believe there are similar pronouncements elsewhere.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But are these quotes being observed on a daily basis?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Are the Ministers themselves all mindful of letting public servants do their jobs professionally and not putting them under political pressure?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This Bill is an attempt to entrench the relationships of accountability and demarcate out-of-bounds markers for Ministers vis-à-vis the public sector agencies.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Workers' Party welcomes this development, after nearly 60 years under the same ruling Party.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Nevertheless, as I have said, I have some doubts and concerns about how the Bill will be operationalised and what appear to be gaps that may allow the Bill's intentions to be circumvented.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It is laudable that efforts have been made to establish a consistent system of governance across public bodies in Singapore as well as to enable a whole-of-Government approach to make policy planning and service delivery more efficient via this Bill.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This is a step in the right direction, especially as we develop Singapore into a data-centric Smart Nation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Corporations are leveraging big data insights to improve their processes and bottom lines and spark innovation, the public sector can also tap on data to identify valuable insights which can be used to develop and enhance initiatives for public good.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: As we recognise data as a valuable strategic asset, we have to ensure that data is not subject to abuse as the data residing in public sector agencies are personal data of our fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I have a few questions arising from these concerns.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: First, could the Minister share some examples of data sharing projects which are envisioned in the promulgation of this Bill, such as which sector agencies are involved in these data sharing projects, what are the objectives of these projects and the types of data that are being shared.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I really hope provision of data and information can be one-stop so that we do not to provide the same piece of information or document to many different Government agencies.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Under what circumstances would a re-identification of anonymised information be required?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: For example, data could be categorised by different levels of sensitivity and different guidelines on collecting, transferring and handling of data would apply to the different categories.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Also, what safeguards are in place to ensure these guidelines are complied with?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: As we embark on developing data-centric digital solutions to enhance service delivery by sector agencies, I would also like to ask the Minister if there is a framework in place to evaluate the costs, benefits and risk of data sharing projects envisioned under this Bill.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Are there are any guidelines for sector agencies to comply with in the implementation of initiatives which require people to engage in a new way with new digital channels?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Take for example, the recent Centrelink debacle in Australia.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Centrelink is an Australian government organisation responsible for administering welfare services.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Centrelink had launched an automated debt recovery system which used data supplied by organisations, such as the Australian Tax Office, to match information recipients gave to Centrelink.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The automated system promised to be more accurate than the manual matching process and would improve the capability for the identification and recovery of debt owed to taxpayers while avoiding mistakes that would adversely affect the recipient’s payments.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: While the system resulted in thousands of debt recovery notices, in a significant portion of cases, there was no debt or the amount had been over-estimated and thousands of clients had to spend many hours and days disputing debts they did not actually owe.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: As clients were only given a three-week deadline to repay the debt, some were forced to repay debt they did not believe they owed because they could not successfully dispute the debt before the deadline.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Service delivery was worsened and this impacted people’s trust in the government organisation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Following a probe into the system, the Commonwealth Ombudsman found that the implementation problems could have been mitigated through better project planning and risk management at the onset.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This includes more rigorous user testing with customers and service delivery staff, a more incremental rollout and better communication to staff and stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The Ombudsman’s report stated that a key lesson for agencies and policymakers when proposing to roll out large-scale measures which require people to engage in a new way with new digital channels, is for agencies to engage with stakeholders and provide resources for manual support during transition periods.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This is a key lesson which we can take reference from as new or enhanced public initiatives are launched further to this Bill.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On the whole, the Bill marks a step in the right direction and I cannot oppose the Bill.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Before I continue, I declare that I serve as the Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of a research and consulting firm that has, on occasion, undertaken public sector projects in the past.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My speech will focus on clause 11 which seeks to limit the Minister's powers to issue directions to public sector agencies so as to reduce the risk of the politicisation of the Public Service.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is clearly a step in the right direction and I welcome this.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Having said that, I share the concerns and support the questions raised in relation to this clause by my colleague and party chairman Sylvia Lim.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I shall not repeat them here but will focus on one additional consideration.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There would always presumably be some public servants who possess the necessary ambition, aspiration and willingness to seek to exit the Public Service and join politics and perhaps to become a Minister or even Prime Minister one day.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So as to increase their chances of successfully joining the ruling Party and becoming MPs or Ministers, such public servants may try to second-guess what their Ministers would like them to do.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even in the absence of any explicit instruction from a Minister to do the said act, they may then just go out and do it.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The intended goal of such a strategy may be for that individual public servant to be looked upon favourably not just by his or her Minister but by the leadership of the ruling Party in respect of consideration for being fielded as a ruling Party candidate in the next election.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My focus is on the principle and managing future risks.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To be sure, there would be nothing illegal about any public servant attempting to pursue such a strategy and this law does not change that.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But is it healthy for Singapore for such a culture to become widespread?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: After all, becoming a Minister is an attractive career option for a high performing public servant as it means taking on the role of the boss under which he or she ultimately serves.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, the incentive for such a culture to grow is there.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And if such a culture takes root in the future, it would mean that the Public Service would become partisan and eventually and inevitably be seen by the public as partisan, which would be a terrible outcome not least in terms of attracting and retaining good public servants who have no wish to be partisan or to eventually enter politics.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To be sure, the risk of subordinates second-guessing their boss and doing what their boss wants in the absence of a formal explicit instruction is not new.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In fact, it is a risk that has been noted for centuries in the context of all kinds of organisations.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I will cite one famous example from history.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is a sentence attributed to a former King of England from the 12th century, Henry II.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: He was supposed to have said in the council of his senior advisors and noblemen, "Will no one rid me of this meddlesome Priest?", referring to Thomas Becket, the then-Archbishop of Canterbury, with whom he had had repeated conflicts.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This was not a direct order, but it is said that, upon hearing this comment, four senior knights attending the meeting then went on to kill Becket in one of the most famous political assassinations of medieval times.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I cannot, of course, attest to the historical veracity of every part of the story but it is a story that has been told through the centuries to illustrate the perils of subordinates in any organisation second-guessing their boss and taking actions that they think may please their boss and even perhaps going to greater extremes than their boss would have thought necessary.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, this problem is not a new one and not specific to any organisation or context.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, how do we prevent a culture of ambitious public servants second-guessing their bosses and take partisan but legally permissible actions which may, over time, tend to erode the reputation of the Public Service for non-partisanship?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The analogy here with what I am proposing is not perfect.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But it is useful to note that there is a precedent for such a mandatory time gap proposal.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: He or she would know that they would need to find employment outside the Public Service in the private sector or not-for-profit sector for some years before joining politics.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hence, there would be a period of time when they would need to find alternative employment and the fruit of their partisan action or actions could not be reaped immediately.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And with the passage of time, the memory of their acts in the Public Service and their links to their former political masters may become more attenuated, thus further reducing the motive to commit such acts in the first place.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Imposing a mandatory time gap may send a signal to aspiring public servants that if they choose to second-guess their bosses and speed the path to a Ministerial post, the link between their actions and the hoped for results will be weaker than it is now.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It may cool the ardour of such public servants to second-guess their boss and act for him or her.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The relative lack of such experience in the Cabinet has often been bemoaned by experts and commentators.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Speaking at a technology conference last September, Deputy CE of GovTech, Mr Chan Cheow Hoe, suggested that the Government has changed its approach to delivering services in the past few years, away from a prescriptive view where "Ministries and the agencies know everything", in his words, to providing what they think "is good for the citizens, and somehow or rather people should accept it" in the past but now "the social contract has changed quite a fair bit".

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: He says, "more and more citizens are very demanding”, and finally concluded that "it is really about understanding what people need at various moments in their life and delivering this service".

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: While I support the Bill’s intent to codify a uniform corporate governance framework for public bodies and the Public Service in the interests of consistency, transparency and efficiency, I have some concerns as to whether the Bill best furthers this aptly termed new "social contract" in public sector governance.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: My concerns are as follows, Mr Deputy Speaker, and allow me to take them in turn.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: One, provisions, such as the Obligation of the Statutory Boards to keep proper accounts and present its audited financial statements to the Minister-in-charge in a timely manner, are straightforward.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Apart from being contained in the Statutory Board's constituent Acts, there should be no question as to whether or not there is an obligation to do so.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The same can be said perhaps of requirements of information sharing, disclosure of certain interests, and submitting budget estimates on time.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: What then, Mr Speaker, has prompted the Ministries to seek to further hard-coding Statutory Board obligations which implement Government policies and deliver public services?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Have any Statutory Boards suggested thus far that they may choose not to comply with a request or direction made by the relevant Ministry in relation to “pertinent subject matter” as envisioned by clause 4(1) because it does not have or carry the force of law?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Three, are there specific instances of public sector governance lapses regarding certain Statutory Boards, such as perhaps the Land Transport Authority (LTA), that have moved the Government to highlight the importance of standardising, formalising and strengthening regulatory oversight?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Have there been recent lapses in financial auditing or reporting to the AGO or other authority that are a cause for concern?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Four, is there any clarification on the mechanism for and the scope of data sharing under clause 6 of the Bill?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Will further guidance be given to both the public sector agency that requests and the one that receives the data, and will any protective measures be available to guard against unwitting data privacy breaches?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Five, could the Minister give examples perhaps to illustrate the broad point that is made in relation to clause 7(2) on when, in certain circumstances, unauthorised data sharing may not be an offence?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Looking at the explanatory note, it suggests that this may not be an offence if the “sharing may have been done on the basis of the common law exception of public interest”, and there could be a further elaboration on this point.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Six, is the position of CE within each public body a new point?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: How is this any different from the current position inferred to the top administrator who helms the very directorate of each Statutory Board?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It says that even if a member of a public body does not disclose a conflict of interest or does not abstain from being involved in decision-making that might benefit him, the public body's decision remains valid.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Will that rob the duty to disclose a conflict of interest of having any real consequence?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Should any decision of the consequences of the failure to disclose not be made by a Public Service administrative tribunal, perhaps even a Court?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Eight, given the importance the Bill appears to place on data sharing for big data analytics, what are the benefits that the Government hopes to reap in sectors perhaps like healthcare, and how will it insulate against the risk of data privacy breaches?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Will whistleblowers within the Public Service be encouraged to come forward?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The Bill focuses on a policy change that the Bill represents but this would be an important component of that policy change.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Individuals will not come forward to volunteer information if they fear that they would attract criticism or blame.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: So, it is essential, in the absence of obvious or serious wrongdoing, to encourage such individuals within the Public Service that there is an "open culture" of sharing and questioning, rather than the culture of blame.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: We heard earlier this morning about Keppel Offshore and Marine's (KOM's) recent cooperation with investigative agencies both in Singapore and abroad.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: But I must say that this comes as small comfort to Singaporeans, who fear that Singapore's image regarding anti-corruption has been irreparably tarnished.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Today, the management of public records falls under the purview of NLB, which controls and directs the National Archives of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: NLB conducts a records management programme that includes the retention and preservation of public records.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: The Board has the authority to decide which records of the Government or another public office are of national or historical significance and should be transferred to the National Archives.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: No records of the Government or another public office may be destroyed or disposed of without the authorisation of the Board.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Nor may any person excise, mark or otherwise deface or send out of the country any public records without the authorisation of the Board.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Many of us tell ourselves that things may be the way they seem now.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: But time lends perspective and, with the proper keeping of public records and, in time, with greater accessibility to them, history can be the judge.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Many agencies currently have their own internal policies and guidelines, but this Bill will provide an overarching legislation and benchmark the standards of governance that should be adhered to.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Examples are, disclosure of interest, proper financial record keeping, budget estimates, annual reports submission and so on.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Can the Minister clarify for us whether some of these will prevail or will they be considered defunct with the new Act in place?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The clarity will be necessary to ensure better compliance and adoption of this Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Clarification as to how it will be aligned with PDPA, where relevant, the scope of the information that will be and can be shared, and the mechanisms of sharing, such as will it be electronic, for example, and what protective measures will this be guided by?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Also, how about compliance with the Protection of Secrecy Acts which Statutory Boards and Government companies have to abide by currently?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Will we be seeing some changes, or will the clauses from this Act need to be incorporated into this new Bill that we are debating today?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: With many steps in our processes in the Public Service involving human factors, we know there is a likelihood of errors happening.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Take, the example, the recent Ministry of Education (MOE) school data leak.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: How can we learn from these incidences and incorporate some of the lessons into policy?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: As across the public sector, there will be more handling of this big data, can the Minister share with us how all this data will be stored?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Will there need to be standalone personal computers or other approved devices?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: How much and which parts of the data are permissible for research purposes?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Also, moving into all these, will there need to be some informed consent, a generic one perhaps, by the public and users of the public services at some point in time?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Will it be the Ministry of Communications and Information (MCI)?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Or what about the the Smart Nation and Digital Government Office?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: So, perhaps some clarification on that as well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: I look forward to these clarifications with this important Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The protection against all and potential abuses and misuse are preventive steps and we have to incorporate these now at the planning stages before the final implementation of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: (In Malay):   Sir, this Public Sector (Governance) Bill seeks to provide a consistent framework and practice amongst Public Service bodies.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I support this Bill but, at the same time, I would like to seek two clarifications.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: (In English): My second clarification is regarding clause 11.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Additionally, I will share two scenarios and would like to ask the Minister to provide his views whether, in these two scenarios, the Public Service entity mentioned has more or less been politicised.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The first scenario, an individual who is a member of the political party and who contested but was defeated in the General Election who is now holding two designations at the same time – one, a branch chairman of a political party and two, as an advisor to grassroots organisation which, in fact, is a position appointed and endorsed by PA's executive board.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Second scenario, a grassroots advisor appointed by PA, a Statutory Board, conducts house visits accompanied by staff of Statutory Boards, such as the HDB, inviting residents to his MPS if residents require him to appeal on their behalf.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Nonetheless, the MPS session is held in a political party branch office by the grassroots advisor who writes referral or appeal letters using a political party letterhead and signs off as the branch chairman of a political party.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Much good can come out of it, if we use it wisely, for example, the directions on data sharing.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: From a social service perspective, data sharing has advantages.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: From the perspective of a client, data sharing enables multiple public bodies serving the same client to construct a holistic profile for more timely and relevant intervention and support.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Data sharing equips public bodies to anticipate the onboarding of a client, prepare the relevant support, and monitor the progress of a client or a former client.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: This will enable public agencies to provide further intervention and further support.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It also saves the client time and effort in having to produce the same information to different public bodies at different times.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: These are some of the advantages from an individual's perspective.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: For public bodies, data sharing enables public bodies to develop more holistic profiles of the clients and their needs, thereby informing policymaking in the planning of services and their delivery, through analytics and research.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It enables public bodies to better understand the trajectory of the clients, which would improve the planning of the respective downstream and upstream services and interventions.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: There are, however, a number of concerns, one of which being how members of the public do not fear the sharing of personal data.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We are very happy to give our identity card number for lucky draws.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We do not realise that the giving of such important pieces of information for not so critical functions or purposes can do a lot of harm to us.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The current provisions, as drafted, cover only unauthorised disclosure or use.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Members of the public, some of us would be concerned with security breaches, including hacking.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Minister also address obligations to report security breaches to the appropriate Minister as well as the requirement to take appropriate steps to remedy the situation as soon as practicable?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Would we consider a provision regulating the manner in which shared data would be used to address concerns of possible discrimination?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Anonymised shared data should be used in a manner that is not discriminatory or stigmatising to persons to whom the data relate.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I have noted the impracticalities of obtaining consent.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Would the Minister clarify if there could be circumstances under which informed consent or opting out may be provided for?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In terms of transparency and accountability, these would also be a big concern.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: How would the Government propose to inform members of the public about the sharing, analysis, use of and access to their personal data?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: For example, some may be afraid of unlawful surveillance.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I hope the Minister would address these concerns.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In determining guidelines for data-sharing, perhaps we could also have reference to the Caldicott principles.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: These are principles in the Caldicott Committee’s Report on the Review of Patient-Identifiable Information.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It is a United Kingdom committee and the report may serve as a reference for us.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: A few of the principles are as follows: the proposed access to, sharing of or use of the information should be justified and only allowed if it is necessary; the amount of identifiable information to be shared should be kept as minimal as possible.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: As noted in the earlier portion of my speech, greater clarity is requested and we hope to hear more from the Minister.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In relation to section 40, I noted the Minister's comments earlier that he would be seeking an amendment at the Committee stage.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I am not sure if the amendments would include section 40.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: If not, I would request for clarification as to the exemption of PA from the requirements of that provision.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Having sought the clarifications, Deputy Speaker, Sir, please allow me to now make some general comments.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It can potentially change the landscape of Public Service agencies in Singapore, creating Public Service agencies more effective and competent than many others in other countries.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: One would have thought that in times like these, given the complexity of the issues facing Singapore, given that it is no longer possible for a single Ministry or a single public agency to adequately address such issues, the Government might wish to enshrine the principle of a whole-of-Government approach to the delivery of services to the Singapore public within the same piece of legislation.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: This would have set a very clear context for the legislation and the implementation to follow.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Somewhat disappointingly, also, this piece of legislation appears to embody the form but not the spirit of public service.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It sets out a framework that is forward-looking and relevant to the complexity of issues faced by our country.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It shows a clear legislative will to hold the public sector to high standards of governance and accountability, and I applaud and commend the Government and the public service sector for initiating and putting the proposed legislation before Parliament.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Public service is not about a set of regulations.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It is about the people within the public service sector, and the people for whom the public sector exists.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Developing and implementing a consistent system of governance and accountability, meeting high standards of accountability are worthy aspirations, soon to be legislated.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: They are fundamental and integral to an effective and impactful Public Service, and they are integral to public trust.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Our end goal is to serve the Singapore public.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Likewise, developing and implementing a whole-of-Government approach in the delivery of services in the Singapore public sector is integral to an effective and impactful Public Service.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Our end goal is to serve the Singapore public.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The second cardinal principle is what gives humanity to our public sector.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It is that which gives us hope for the future.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It is that which assures us that our public sector will do that which is right and good for Singapore, regardless of political masters, regardless of vociferous demands from the public.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Without the spirit of public service, we will be an AI administration − clean, efficient, clinical.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: But we know that compliance with a set of rules does not make an honest or effective public service agency.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Efficiency alone will not, in every case, serve our people well.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It is a scrupulous adherence to the integrity of regulations and a conscientious adherence to the welfare of our people that will make our Public Service honest and effective – human.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Let our Public Service continue to serve our people with conviction, commitment, courage, professionalism and empathy.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Always fearless to do that which is right and good, yet exercising humility, empathy and kindness.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Then and only then are we a public sector, a Government, able to meet the highest accountability standards to our people.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Malay):   Mr Deputy Speaker, to my understanding, MUIS is not really affected by this amendment.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I support this amendment that guarantees the standards of administration and governance for each of our public agencies because it ensures that quality as well as accountability and transparency standards continue to be upheld.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At the same time, there are some suggestions within this amendment that are already familiar to MUIS, which already possesses and implemented accountability and transparency standards, which were determined by the Government under the Administration of Muslim Law Act (AMLA).

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The appointment of MUIS' CE is still based on the MUIS Council's approval with the Minister's concurrence.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This ensures that the amendment does not erode the responsibility or influence of MUIS Council members regarding the appointment of the CE that is based on the experience and expertise of each MUIS Council member.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would also like to acknowledge the support and funding by the Government for the corporate and administrative functions of MUIS, which have allowed MUIS to channel money from donations and zakat from the Muslim community towards the community's other needs.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, this is an important Bill to consolidate the different Acts governing the various public sector bodies.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, I have a couple of concerns for clarification.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, this sharing of data and information needs to be made expedient, efficient and transparent not just between public sector agencies but also within each agency, between their different departments and units.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There have been instances where the different departments and units within one public sector agency do things in silo and are not cognisant of what the other departments and units within that same public sector agency are doing.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For instance, I have received feedback from residents about their experience when executing the purchase or sale of their flats, in securing housing loans from HDB, or in managing the funds related to housing through CPF Board.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
