text: There have been occasions where residents lamented while they have been approved their housing loan through the housing finance department, but when executing the sale or purchase of the flat through the sales department, there seems to be a lack of information sharing between the departments.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This has made the transaction experience faced by residents nothing short of frustrating and confusing.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For some residents I have met, their home loan eligibility approval or extension by the housing finance department has not been conveyed to the sales department, which then requires them to make additional CPF cash payment instead during the sale or purchase transaction for their flat.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Another example is the sharing of information by MOE with Institutes of Higher Learning or self-help organisations, such as the Council for the Development of the Singapore Malay/Muslim Community (MENDAKI), the Chinese Development Assistance Council (CDAC), the Singapore Indian Development Association (SINDA) or the Eurasian Association (EA).

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Having been involved in a self-help organisation and a couple of public sector institutions, it is a common refrain heard amongst strategic planners or managers that a more open sharing of student and cohort education-related information would be useful in designing and implementing programmes or interventions by the self-help groups that can better help our students.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The sharing and use of information and data within each and across public sector agencies will make it more efficient and effective in helping Singaporeans address their healthcare, housing, education or social and financial assistance needs.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, to what extent will the sharing of information or data make this possible?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will Singaporeans find it easier to purchase a flat and secure a housing loan at the same time?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Or visit their choices of doctors across different restructured hospitals and have their medical information shared?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Or have access to the necessary social or financial assistance without having to repeatedly provide their personal or family information to different Public Service officers?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, from what I understand, the removal of the CE can be solely decided by the Minister.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There seems to be a lot of power vested in the Minister to decide on the removal of the CE from a public sector agency.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Sufficient consideration to be made regarding the CE's prior experience, background or contributions to the agency should be considered collectively and consultatively, rather than largely by the Minister alone.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The requirement for accountability and clear responsibility would support the greater whole-of-Government approach.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Along with Smart Nation drive, citizens should have a single platform access to relevant information on Government policies.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The changes to the Bill also signal a timely need to have better data control for more efficient and effective processes.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: On corporate governance, generally, the public has high regard for the Singapore Public Service.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It is well-known for its efficiency in terms of its rules, practices and processes.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: However, at times, Government agencies run into excessive bureaucracy when working with one another.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, it is important for our Public Service to keep up to date on their rules, practices and processes to continuously uphold public trust and confidence.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Some of the practices and processes could be irrelevant in the current context and, with a digital economy as the future, the public sector should embrace digitisation wherever possible and reflect them in their practices and processes.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: On data governance, we often hear the word, "Big Data" as we move towards a digital economy.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Data collected can be used to make more informed decisions and formulate policies more effectively.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Financial governance is related to corporate governance and it is extremely pertinent to have proper management of financial resources.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: There should be clarity on who is responsible and accountable for what matters.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Statutory Boards should work closely with their respective Ministries to implement Government policies and deliver public services effectively so that public confidence is further strengthened.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: There should also be rigorous financial reporting, in compliance with the AG.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: There must also be a fine balance between rigidity and flexibility, as well as simplicity, to minimise bureaucracy.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: These would not have been possible without the vision and the good governance from our forefathers.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Like many other young Singaporeans, I want this going for Singapore to SG100 and beyond.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As the global environment changes, so has our country.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Some things can no longer remain status quo. "Good" is probably insufficient at times; more often, we need more than "good".

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But I believe it is this changing new world and its challenges that help define us and even bring new dimensions to nation-building.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: If we continue to adapt, raise the bar and challenge what we are able to achieve and be guided by good governance, both the public sector and as citizens, Singapore can continue to shine brightly.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: For this to be maintained, we need to do more and better each time.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: So, what exactly is better or best in governance?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I do not think there is a single definition or milestone that fully embodies what governance is.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: In my view, I would consider better governance as one that is strategic, forward-looking, continues to adjust or set new benchmarks befitting the circumstances and has effective ground implementation with proper accountability.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This Bill has set out some aspects of this nature but I would like to highlight three areas for consideration by the Public Service.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: One, encourage a more positive culture and accountability.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: With the many years of public service in Singapore, it is undeniable that a positive working culture does exist.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Through my interactions with the agencies, I have worked with good-minded Public Service individuals who go the extra mile for the community.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Given the complexity of projects moving ahead, we need even stronger cooperation and coordination among the inter-agencies, from planning to implementation.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: For better implementation, it will be best when one of the agencies can take the lead and be responsible in any joint project.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It is critical for clear accountability, and necessary should there be no revolving doors.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This is also equally applicable to Government-linked companies.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Public service workers should be encouraged to give their best of ways and not worry that their actions are not the usual approach.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: In public service, it is the results and the positive impact on the community that matter and not the process.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Increasingly, there are more challenges that we will encounter which may never be prescribed or previously documented.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: We need the working level in the Public Service to be empowered and supported to take such initiatives.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: There is no absolute right or wrong approach in the Public Service.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Each needs to be tried and adapted to the needs of the target group for their purpose.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This is also the spirit that we are trying to promote in schools and inculcate in our young to try and know that it is okay to fail.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: What happens if one of the pathways to be covered is not a frequently used route by pedestrians?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Or what if it is known that there are future works currently in planning that may require this covered pathway to be taken down within a short time after it is installed?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Should the works still proceed as the contract has been awarded or should it be partially deferred for the future?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: On the same note, some of the works involve various agencies as it encompasses matters ranging from underground utilities to the trees.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Without proper cross-coordination in its implementation, the disamenity created can be huge and constant.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: With better coordinated planning and implementation among these agencies, I believe we can look forward to reducing wastage of resources.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: With that, I mean finance, time and workers.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Additionally, this can enable the lead agency to have the ability to stop or reprioritise projects if the objectives or needs have changed.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: To be accountable for public services, we need the courage to pull the plug or make changes as projects progress and not continue when the final impact on the public is less than desired.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The digital world has changed our lives, the lives of every common man.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Has the digital world made our lives better or worse?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I think it is up to us to leverage the best and harness the power of digitalisation.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Every individual has their rights to decide if information should be provided and be respectfully protected.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: When the PDPA was introduced, I felt it was a great move.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: PDPA gave individuals the choice to opt out of communications they found irrelevant and what not to be shared.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As our population ages, how can we encourage more of such initiatives to assist the elderly to age within our community?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: For more effective outreach, there will come a point when it is difficult for the Ministries to roll out more programmes on the ground solely with internal resources, especially if it requires intense, frequent follow-up with the individuals.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: How then can we harness external resources, for example, the ground-up voluntary groups, the voluntary welfare organisations (VWOs), beyond the Ministries to assist the needy and vulnerable in our society without infringing their privacy through sharing of data, knowledge or relevant information?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: With time, our society has become more plural and diverse.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It is a fact that we have to embrace and adapt our policies to.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Governance is no longer restricted to the public sector.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It requires our citizens to be a part of the process.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The more our citizens take an active role in it, the more effective our implementation will likely be and plausible for future changes to take place.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As mentioned earlier, Ministry-led community projects being one such example.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The quantity of programmes is a poor indicator of quality and effectiveness of outreach.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: At times, it competes for the same pool of resources.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It may also result in our inability to scale up on programmes and only having to scrap and replace with yet another programme.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Thus, we should utilise the community knowledge and data-driven approach to strengthen our social safety net.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Moving forward, how can we enable our citizens to become communicators and partners of future policies on the ground?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: While setting major strategic directions of a country continues to be the Government’s role, our citizens can take an active role in discussion and feedback on community and societal topics.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: First, increase the depth and exposure of our school-going children to our Constitution and policymaking process earlier in the education curriculum.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Let them understand what the various committees represent and do, how and what the annual Budget actually means to their lives.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Lastly, increase the current local training and communication of policies through dialogues by the public servants to the local community.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: While we are thankful for what the public servants have been doing, we need to look beyond the current.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Encourage more to think out of the box, take initiatives, be comprehensive, thorough and thoughtful throughout the service delivery.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Should this mean the public sector has to change and adjust where required to meet the current times, we have to do it.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: If new yardsticks, new measures must be put in place to better protect and account for public funds, service interaction and so on, this must be continuously reviewed, redesigned and implemented.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Likewise, we, too, hope that our citizens will play their part as we build our nation and be encouraged to volunteer, build a sense of ownership and belonging for Singapore, and fellow citizens demonstrate active citizenry and, therefore, they should have the options to embark on this journey with us sooner.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This two-way process should be the mark of our continuous engagement and fundamentals of our nation-building as we progress.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: With this, I support the Bill and hope the Public Service sector continues to uphold the standards and raise the bar to greater heights.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I stand in support of all the provisions and amendments to the Bill but would like to urge the Government to pay special attention to two key aspects which I feel are at the heart of corporate governance, which are quality of leadership and transparency in the area of accountability.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I have witnessed this first-hand when I served as a board member on IMDA from 2010 to 2016.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, some are not, in my view, given the opportunity to fully test their potential in their brief stints at the various Statutory Boards.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: In some sectors, these CEOs – and members of their leadership teams – are rotated perhaps a little too frequently.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: In certain sectors, might we consider a longer stint for CEOs?

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps feedback from industry and small and medium enterprises (SMEs) in the various sectors could be used when deciding on leadership and succession.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, there will be some leaders who will be exceptional in whichever industry they may be placed, but such leaders are few and far between, even in the corporate world.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: By and large, leaders need time to understand the industry, its people and culture.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Leaders could spend up to three years to fully comprehend the complexities of the sectors they operate in, before they can even begin to make an impact.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Each time a Statutory Board CEO is rotated, it is like hitting a reset button: industry leaders would have to rebuild relationships and reorientate each new CEO, and SMEs in the industry would have to start building the relationship from scratch again.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: And as good as the new CEO may be, there will be industry initiatives that are left in limbo while he or she comes up to speed.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: For a good six months to a year, things would not move, because it is not just the CEO who is learning the ropes.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: It is also his or her management team, because these appointments would also be rotated, though at different times.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: What we need to avoid, Mr Deputy Speaker, is a mentality that these rotating appointments are treated as a rite of passage that would lead almost automatically to bigger and better things.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Breeding a culture of ambition, apathy and fleeting commitment impacts the quality of leadership in our Statutory Boards and has serious implications for corporate governance and Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: We want leaders who will observe the spirit and principles of good governance outlined in this Bill.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: But beyond this, we must aim to groom leaders who will shape the future of good governance, leaders who will have the industry insights, experience, relationships, perhaps some "battle scars" to speak from positions of credibility, respect and trust.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: And they can only do this if they have spent enough time to fully understand the business and the community they operate in.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I feel that the boards of Statutory Boards should also be made more accountable for the performance of the entities they lead.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: For if we are to truly embrace private sector practices – and not just borrow chunks that we might deem useful – we must also hold our boards and CEOs accountable when Statutory Boards run afoul of corporate governance.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: When we have seen leaders of Statutory Boards fail to deliver, or act improperly, the Government has always been very swift in acknowledging and rectifying mistakes.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: However, it is not always clear what becomes of the errant leaders and Boards that were in place when these mistakes were made.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: This leads to unwarranted speculation that leaders are just rotated to another Statutory Board or Government position.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: However, it is also important that in aiming to improve corporate governance, it does not create more layers of guidelines, rules and regulations that will surely stifle creativity and growth.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Disruption and the digital revolution have shown that conventional approaches can quickly become obstacles to growth.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: So, while we must uphold corporate governance at all times, we should also be nimble enough to work fast and smart and be free of red tape.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Billion-dollar businesses are now being hatched, as we speak, in dormitory rooms and teenage bedrooms.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: In staying true to the spirit of good governance, we must also be fast enough to ride these waves of innovation in areas that are unchartered.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I am hopeful that the provisions of this Bill, as well as greater attention to the quality of leadership and transparency in accountability in our Statutory Boards, will augur well for corporate governance in our public sector.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Establishing a system of governance with greater accountability and transparency in our public sector is welcomed.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I support the Bill’s objective, which aspires to remove independent vertical units, commonly known as silos, and create a whole-of-Government connected approach to delivering public services.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have comments and queries on one fundamental aspect of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As illustration, clause 4(1) confers powers on the Minister to give directions to all Singapore Public Sector Agencies.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This principle behind clause 4 is to enable a whole-of-Government approach in the implementation of policy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Hence, clause 4(2)(g) specifically qualifies that such directions can only be made for purposes of supporting a whole-of-Government approach.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In this case, then it seems logical and consistent to ensure clause 4(1) applies to the Public Service as well.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The exclusion of the Public Service can be seen in clauses complementary to clause 4, namely, clauses 9, 10 and 11.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This exclusion is also present in clause 6 on data-sharing, and clauses in Part 4 and Part 5 of the Bill on governance and financial administration of public bodies.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, these entities serve very important functions and impact everyday citizens.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that all organisations, public or private, have a hierarchical structure and contain layers of structures.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: At times, one layer may be more deeply embedded, resulting in a silo structure.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: At times, such a silo structure is necessary for administrative purposes or for the very functioning of an organisation, such as the military's chain of command.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Applying this line of logic, I foresee a possible rationale for the exclusion of the Public Service – on justification that these five agencies exercise very specialised powers and fulfil very specific, critical functions within our society such that their constituting Act already contains provisions allowing the Minister to directly make directions, or an informal tight governance framework may currently be in place, or that these five agencies need the flexibility and autonomy to have room to exercise discretionary powers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, this justification would similarly apply to other Public Bodies, which similarly have constituting Acts containing internal controls.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There are still quite a number of "walls" among our Government departments.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I think some of these exist for good reasons, such as to ensure that only necessary information is shared on a "need to know" basis, for confidentiality and to protect personal privacy.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, for a family in financial difficulties, they can expect appropriate and timely allocation of assistance due to better coordination of the sources of assistance.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I note that agencies, such as HDB, the Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA), LTA and the Traffic Police, could have maintained different records of traffic offences under their respective areas of responsibility, although there are similarities in some of the areas of responsibility.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Similarly, will his or her records with other enforcement agencies or Ministries, such as the National Environment Agency (NEA) and the Ministry of Manpower, be consolidated?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Overcoming the challenges posed by the current walls among Government departments is one thing.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: More often than not, there are many exchanges and overlaps between information and data held by Government agencies and non-Government-related bodies.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These include information which have to be requested from or extracted from private entities.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: An example of such situations are medical records.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, in situations where Government bodies have to provide information to private entities in order to enable certain transactions and the provision of certain goods and services, how would the Government ensure the safety and privacy of such information?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The personnel guilty of this are the very ones charged with keeping the information safe – the IT staff.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This can happen in both Government and non-Government entities.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With that, I conclude with my support for the Bill.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There were quite a few questions citing specific clauses and sub-clauses, and fairly technical.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I will try my best to answer them all.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Ms Thanaletchimi is right to say that there is a balance between central control as well as getting our Statutory Boards to have flexibility and autonomy, and creativity and innovation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And this is a balance that we have to strike between effective governance, policy consistency on one hand and operational autonomy on the other hand.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is the same when a manager runs a department of a few people.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: You want to give the staff the space to take initiative, run with it, work with different people, but they are still your staff.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And you meet them once in a while to give them support and direction.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Every year, it is good HR practice also to do appraisal and coach them on their development.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And, when something goes wrong, you still have to answer for the staff as department head.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, the same principles apply to Statutory Boards.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But for operational matters, it is better for Statutory Boards to have autonomy, tapping on board members.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And I agree with Mr Ganesh Rajaram that Board members can do more and be more active in helping the governance and running of the Statutory Board and ensuring that the Board members are from different backgrounds, experience and skills that they can bring to the table.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These are the layers that we have to put in place to make sure a Statutory Board is run well.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In answer to Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan, this Bill is really not in response to any Government lapses, incidents or confusion on the part of public servants, or that there are instances where Statutory Boards refuse to comply with a Government direction.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I have mentioned some of it in my Second Reading speech.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: One, for the lack of a better word, it is really neatness, really just neatness.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Today, we have over 60 Statutory Boards operating in an increasingly complex and disrupted environment, facing challenges that no single agency can tackle alone.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The continued need for Statutory Boards to be governed well and work together to provide better public service is all the more pressing.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Specifically, on the clause for Ministers to give direction, they are present in all Acts but they are written slightly differently with different conventions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There are no good reasons why they are different, other than they were written and passed at different times in history.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, we centralise them into one central Act.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is now clear, transparent, neat and, should we find the need and justification to amend them in future, the amendment will also be transparent and more effective.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Where there are substantive changes from today, I have highlighted them in my Second Reading speech.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Not that they are not doing so now.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But we are now hardcoding this and, in so doing, make our direction clear.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Two, is the setting up of a data-sharing regime that I spoke about.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan specifically asked if the term "CE" is a new one mentioned in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It does refer to the CEO at the apex job within the Statutory Board.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Ganesh Rajaram asked about the tenure of the CEO and whether postings are too frequent.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is a point that we constantly have to wrestle within the Public Service.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is really not part of this Bill but we do have to balance between someone staying long, having the experience and stability but, at the same time, they can get entrenched, versus bringing in somebody with new perspectives and innovative ideas.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And what the Member raised is a pertinent point and we will continue to consider this very carefully.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I agree with Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan that the broader point is that our system of governance must be one that allows us to constantly work together, recognise problems and improve.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: What we do not want is a culture of witch hunt and blame.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Our approach has always been to look honestly at our flaws and focus our attention on improvements.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And I think this is the culture we want.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Ms Chia Yong Yong said the Public Service goes much beyond just running day to day.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is much beyond efficiency but also about service to people with kindness and humanity.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, likewise, if we want to bring about such a culture, it goes beyond legislation, but also ensuring that the ethos, the spirit, is in every single Public Service agency and that the culture and ethos are upheld.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Most important of all, to uphold these are the leaders, leaders across the various levels of the Public Service, the type of people we bring in, how we make them work together, learn from one another and uphold the values.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We will continue to place great emphasis on this.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is raised by Mr Zaqy Mohamad, Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef, Dr Intan Mokhtar and Miss Cheryl Chan.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I agree it is important to coordinate well amongst public sector agencies as challenges become more complex.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This Bill actually sends a strong signal on the importance of cross-agency coordination.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As to how to ensure strong coordination among agencies and reduce wastage, I think all agencies simply need to work harder, eyes open, ears up and be more creative, more innovative, more citizen-centric.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That is a point that Miss Cheryl Chan and Dr Intan Mokhtar have both raised.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And we have seen many such improvement projects.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For example, Master Planning Committee coordinates infrastructure projects.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It allows 80 agencies to come together on a single platform to provide authoritative location information and services.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Some of the examples that Members mentioned are coordination within the departments and they simply need to sort them out.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But they are really outside of this Bill and you do not need this Bill to have them sorted out.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But in my capacity as the Minister helping out with driving public sector innovation, if you observe any of these, please let me know and I will be most happy to take them up.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These are raised by Mr Louis Ng, Ms Sylvia Lim, Ms Chia Yong Yong and Dr Intan Mokhtar.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: First, the Bill does not prescribe the form of directions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It should not, as Acts that are overly prescriptive rapidly get out of date.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Given the purposes for which directions may be given and the subject matter they are to cover, the form of directions will likely be in formal instruments.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Ms Sylvia Lim mentioned two types of directions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: First, as she correctly said, are really central Ministry issues − governance issues concerning HR and finance.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These typically come in the form of circulars and they are signed by the Permanent Secretaries.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I would say the Bill does not prescribe this, but the typical way the Ministries work − for many years and decades, that is how they work − is that there is brainstorming between political officeholders and staff, including Statutory Board staff, because we have to take into account implementation issues.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: When it is all discussed and we have certain consensus, staff papers are put up with all the views, considerations, options and recommendations incorporated and the many angles covered.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For bigger issues, they might go to the Cabinet.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Decisions are made, and then conveyed through notes of meeting, through to the Statutory Boards, and then it is followed up that way.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It has been done this way for years.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For those coming from the private sector, this is quite a big adjustment.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In the private sector, documentation is not done so diligently.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But trust me, nothing in the Civil Service is decided through WhatsApp and, worse, through emoticons.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is merely an extension of the principle in clause 5.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Louis Ng asked about the scope of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The Civil Service, SAF, SPF, SCDF, Legal Service are all part of Ministries and departments.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, the governance requirements of this Bill apply to them.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There are many references and definitions in this Bill, so it is a bit confusing to read.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I put on record the governance requirements of this Bill apply to them.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Likewise, the protection under clause 11, which Ms Sylvia Lim asked about, extends to every Singapore public sector agency, too.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: However, for certain clauses, the Civil Service, SAF, SPF, SCDF and the Legal Service are excluded, because they are already formally subject to central policy governance requirements that are before this Bill.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For example, these agencies have to comply with Government Instruction Manuals.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For the appointment of the heads of Ministries, that is, Permanent Secretaries, the Constitution already provides a framework where appointments are made by the President, acting in accordance with the advice of the Prime Minister, from a list of names submitted by PSC.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Dr Intan Mokhtar asked about removal of the CE.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Although the Bill does not spell out the exact processes but, for a CE, the apex post of a Statutory Board, to be removed, that is a serious matter and, certainly, a lot of consultation, even before that, if it is for performance-related reasons, coaching, counselling, that all has to take place.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Even removing a Public Service officer is a serious matter, what more a CE.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Ms Chia Yong Yong asked a specific question whether PA is to be exempted from clause 40.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Faisal Manap asked about finance-related provisions that pertain to MUIS in clauses 34 to 41.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: While MUIS is, indeed, exempted from these provisions of the Bill, it is not exempted from similar financial administrative requirements because all these requirements are currently already spelt out and covered by MUIS' constituting Act, namely, AMLA.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We decided there is no need to duplicate them in this Bill.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Now let me move to the topic of clause 11.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Ms Sylvia Lim, Mr Chen Show Mao and Mr Leon Perera asked about this.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Clause 5 standardises the power of the responsible Ministers to give directions to their Statutory Boards, and clause 4 formalises the requirements for Statutory Boards to comply with central policies.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And clause 11 of the Bill presents safeguards to limit the effect of these Ministerial directions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The legal requirement to abide by Ministerial direction is not new at all.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is found in the constituting Acts of most of our Statutory Boards.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But with this Bill, we have a separate and centralised legislation to provide for this.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, it becomes necessary to have clause 11 to make it clear that Ministerial directions do not trump other provisions in the Statutory Board legislation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is a very logical thing to do for legal officers drafting this Bill.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There are a few key points to this clause.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For example, the Minister charged with the responsibility for Government records and archives − a point that Mr Chen Show Mao asked about − can direct Statutory Boards to comply with central policies on the treatment of public records.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But these policies must be consistent with the provisions in the National Library Board (NLB) Act on the role of the National Archives in the treatment of public records.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For example, the Minister’s direction to the Singapore public sector agencies cannot authorise the destruction of public documents without the authorisation of NLB, much less destroy a particular archival document.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To do so would be inconsistent with the NLB Act.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Ms Sylvia Lim asked for further elaboration on this.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: A statutorily independent function is a function which is required by law to be performed independently.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The obvious example is the exercise of judicial functions by the Judiciary.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But we also have Statutory Boards like the Civil Aviation Authority of Singapore, the Maritime and Port Authority or IMDA.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They are vested with the discretion to issue or revoke a licence based on criteria set out in their own legislation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As for a quasi-judicial function, that is a function expected by the law to be discharged, taking into account the facts of the case.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Some of our Statutory Boards have those powers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For example, a disciplinary committee constituted under the Estate Agents Act has the power to decide if there is sufficient cause for disciplinary action against an estate agent "according to the circumstances of the case".

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For example, a Minister cannot direct the award of a procurement contract to any particular tenderer, because that is specific to a case or a person; or to license a particular applicant; or to employ a particular person.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And for that matter, he cannot ask the Police to arrest a certain person, and I hope Ms Sylvia Lim is not suggesting that this is happening.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In fact, the Police Force Act makes that quite clear.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is SPF that has the powers to apprehend offenders.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, if you look at the Skills Development Fund (SDF) fraud case that happened which I answered earlier, I am flabbergasted.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I want the culprits to face the full consequences of the law, but I cannot ask the Police or anybody to arrest them.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We report through SkillsFuture Singapore (SSG) to the Police, the Police investigate and, if they deem fit, the Police arrest them.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That is the way things have been done and will be done.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Having said that, in my years of public service, I have not come across an impasse between Ministers and public servants on this point.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If there is, a public servant who feels any pressure from Ministers can report to their Permanent Secretary, or to the Head of the Civil Service, even the PSC, or even the Corrupt Practices Investigation Bureau, if the case warrants it, and I am sure they know how to follow up.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And I would say, in a typical month, Ministers would have handled hundreds, maybe even thousands, of individual cases coming to us.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Each is appealing for a licence to be given, for an Employment Pass to be given, or whatever the case may be.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And the discipline all these years has been we write them down as appeal cases, lay out the facts of the cases, send them back to the Ministries, the staff still process them based on the grounds and the circumstances of the case.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But ultimately, they have to run the individual appeal cases through the system to be processed.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, clause 11 merely puts a long-standing and existing practice into law.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If a Minister comes across a case that highlights the deficiencies in a system, or an act that should be illegal turns out to be legal, then there is a flaw in the system or in the law.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Then, it is incumbent upon Ministers to review and improve the system, together with the agencies under his charge.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think for civil servants to be politicised in the context of this Bill means to be specifically put under pressure to decide on a specific case.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Faisal Manap then went on to talk about a certain Advisor.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I assume it is a constituency that the Member knows, that a certain candidate lost and then continued to operate on the ground.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But, really, based on the definition I gave, this has nothing to do with this Bill.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If there is any specific complaint that the Member would like to raise, he could raise it with our Deputy Chairman of PA, Minister Chan Chun Sing.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: He has mentioned in this House before that the role of an Advisor has to be very clear.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is to serve the community, it is to foster cohesion in the community.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If they overstep into politics and the Member has reasons to believe so, then please raise it with him.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I am sure he will look into it.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Leon Perera gave a narrative about civil servants who have aspirations to be Ministers, therefore, they second-guessed the Ministers to be in their good books and, in the process, become partisan and, therefore, should we not impose garden leave for civil servants that decide to enter politics?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think there are many problems with what he said.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: First, second-guessing is now a bit of a dirty word.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But if you think about it, in all our work, we do have to anticipate what are the needs of our customers, what are the needs of the people we work with.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is very reasonable for civil servants not to be sycophantic but to understand what is the Ministerial direction, what is the agenda of this Government, how is it shaping up, what are the key priorities, and able to work with the Ministers to develop policies in those directions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I mean, if the Member wants to put it in a negative sense, it is up to him.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But I think there is value for public servants to do that.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And for that matter, for anyone working, to do that.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And I think consultants, too, have to anticipate and maybe second-guess their customers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And whether they then become partisan, I hope the Member is not suggesting that civil servants are partisan, because the conduct and ethos of civil servants are articulated clearly in the IM, that they cannot be politically pressurised.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They have to act neutral and in the interest of the public.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Therefore, do we then have garden leave for civil servants who then go on and maybe join politics?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And the Member draws the analogy with the financial sector.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In the case of MAS and the financial sector, MAS is a regulator, whereas the regulatee is a commercial profit-seeking entity.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, to prevent a conflict of interest, we do not want an MAS officer to be offered a job by a regulatee while he is still at the job at the regulator.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Therefore, you have a garden leave so that you minimise the chances of that happening.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Garden leave is widely practised across financial regimes in the world.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: When we come to the Civil Service and political officeholders, neither one regulates the other, and neither is a commercial profit-seeking entity.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The Member felt that garden leave will help the civil servant think more carefully before joining politics.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think anyone, not just civil servants, joining politics today thinks very, very deeply about it, and spends a long time deliberating that with their families and friends before they are prepared to come in.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is really a calling, as the Member would know.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Zaqy Mohamad, Mr Patrick Tay and Ms Chia Yong Yong asked about data-sharing, the scope and benefits.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I have mentioned this in my Second Reading speech.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These will translate broadly into two kinds of initiatives.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: One, better delivery of services to the individual.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This will inevitably have to involve sharing of identifiable and personal data, and Mr Patrick Tay asked for some examples.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Improving social assistance programmes or removing repeated filling of forms when applying for Government programmes.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I spoke about this during the Second Reading speech.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Where feasible, as Mr Zaqy Mohamad has suggested, specific details need not be shared if they are not needed for the task.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For example, when you apply for financial assistance, data can be shared between other agencies and the processing officer, and they can come in the form of whether do they meet or not meet the criteria and not necessarily tell you how much they earn.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That can surely be done and it will be a good practice.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It can also involve not personal data, but information that each agency holds, which, when put together, offers much better value, such as One-Map, which I mentioned earlier.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For example, when deciding where to build certain facilities, we want to understand the concentration of different segments of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There is no need to know personal details in this instance.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, to decide whether to build a senior activity centre, for example, the relevant agency only needs to know the aggregate number of seniors living in the block or in various precincts.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It can also be about correlating data to derive deeper policy insights.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We intend to set up such centres where central oversight would mitigate the risks of failing to anonymise data.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This Bill is also in alignment with PDPA.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They need to share data and information with one another to best serve the public.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This Bill will significantly improve the protection and safeguard of such shared data.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: First level, it allows existing data-sharing practices to be formalised, such as sharing identifiable information for service delivery and enforcement functions and using only anonymised information for policymaking and planning.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Second level, by articulating the responsibility of each party involved in the data-sharing, it ensures that the same high level of responsibility for data protection is borne by all agencies.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, it is now clear that the agency that uses the data is responsible for protecting and safeguarding it.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We will be able to redress the current misalignment of incentives, where the owner of data is still responsible.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These include the unauthorised disclosure and improper use of information, and, specifically, the unauthorised re-identification of anonymised data.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The Bill did provide for the flexibility for re-identification of data.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That is to deal with contingencies, such as when source agencies’ data is corrupted or destroyed.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: When that happens, re-identification of anonymised data may be performed in order to continue to deliver services to citizens.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The purpose of the Bill is not to pave the way for a future where Government knows everything about everyone, and every misdeed everyone committed is all consolidated.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think there was a question by Mr Gan Thiam Poh.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If ever there was such an initiative, it would have to be explained as to why and for what purpose and for what value.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And decision-making, be it for policy, licence or grant application, is all reduced to data processing and AI algorithm.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In fact, it will be quite a sad state.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If that happens, civil servants will all lose their jobs because we only need computers and software.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, in response to what Mr Patrick Tay said, yes, there are algorithms in various software – which will be tested and audited − but when it comes to decision-making, there must be human intervention, supervision and judgement all the time.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Ms Chia Yong Yong asked for greater clarity on data-sharing initiatives.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I hope Members will feel assured that, today, there is a high level of transparency and public discourse in policy implementation and public service delivery in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If there is a new service to be delivered, such as recently we hear that HDB has an initiative to halve the processing time for transaction of resale flats, it will be announced, and how it will be done will be explained.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And I read the whole explanation in the papers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For more significant initiatives, such as MOH's current initiative to set up a National Electronic Health Record (NEHR) system, they have to do this properly.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, a separate consultation is being held, new legislation needs to be debated and enacted in this House to protect the users of this system.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There is one more question by Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: He asked when unauthorised data-sharing may not be an offence.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The common law already permits sharing of information among public sector agencies where there is public interest.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The Bill does not allow the data-sharing direction to displace the application of common law, nor does the data-sharing direction seek to do this.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It will instead be providing the much-needed practical guidance and certainty on what circumstances would be considered public interest without being exhaustive.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, while the Bill criminalises data-sharing other than in accordance with the data-sharing direction, clause 7(2) allows a defence where sharing is authorised or allowed by "other law".

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That "other law" is a reference to the common law.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For example, it can be shared in order to respond to, say, a life-and-death situation of an individual or in times of a natural disaster or any kind of disaster where contact tracing is required.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It does not include the sharing of data with parties outside of the Public Service, such as VWOs, healthcare providers or private and commercial entities.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But that does not mean today we do not share data with parties outside of the Public Service at all.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We do so when there are clear justifications to improve the public service or to improve service to the public.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For example, to help a student from a dysfunctional family, MOE has to work hand-in-hand with VWOs, self-help groups or Family Service Centres, and, inevitably, personal data has to be shared with all these partners.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Or we share aggregate datasets with research institutes to conduct research and analysis for the Government.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Further, data shared with entities outside of the Public Service and designated for service delivery are bound by confidentiality agreements, with contractual terms that prescribe data protection requirements, and these entities are also bound by PDPA and the Official Secrets Act.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Volunteers are also bound by strict confidentiality agreements and educated on the appropriate use of the data.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Specifically, on the sharing of medical data within the healthcare sector, again, this is beyond the scope of this Bill because restructured hospitals are not defined as part of the Public Service.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MOH is embarking, as I mentioned this earlier, on the NEHR initiative, consulting the public and tabling a Healthcare Services Bill to enable it to do so, to achieve better health outcomes and yet safeguard the interest of patients.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Having said that, it is true that when this Bill is passed, the framework that governs the sharing of data within the Public Service will be improved and better than that for sharing with entities outside of the Public Service, specifically in areas, such as the responsibility to safeguard and protect data.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, the framework will be available and set up for the Public Service, but it will not be extended to sharing outside of the Public Service.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is something that we should look at and we will review and consider if further legislation is required.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Zaqy Mohamad asked a question about data accuracy and verification.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The Government also relies on citizens to verify their own information.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MyInfo, the platform mentioned earlier, allows citizens to amend certain personal information and this information will be shared for transactional services that the Government provides.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This ensures that all agencies are using accurate information on the individual based on his latest update.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Zaqy Mohamad, Ms Chia Yong Yong and Mr Gan Thiam Poh also asked about storage and security.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Government data is stored in Government systems which are protected against breach.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There are various measures we have undertaken to protect data.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Every civil servant/public officer can only access data he is allowed access to.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Access rights will continue to be prescribed based on security clearance and data is only accessed when there is a legitimate purpose or need.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The Government continues to calibrate IT security policies accordingly, such as having proper access control and the role-based access of data based on its classification.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is also likely to lead to improper use or unauthorised disclosures of data which are new criminal offences under this Bill.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Existing measures to ensure that public servants do not use privileged access to information for their personal gain will continue to apply.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For example, all public servants have to declare annually their interests in investments and properties.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For ex-public servants, the Official Secrets Act (OSA), already requires that they do not retain information once they leave service and they are culpable, too, under OSA, if they commit any data-related offence in this Bill.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The provisions in the Protection of Secrecy Act remain valid and relevant for Statutory Boards and prescribed Government companies to abide by, and will be a complementary safeguard to this new Bill.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Minister Ong, your time limit is almost up.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And five, education, because the weakest link is always the human.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We always need to educate every single officer on how to do the right thing so that cybersecurity breaches are minimised, and this must include the reporting of malpractices, as mentioned by Ms Chia Yong Yong.
